entries.title: Iran warns countries against joining US 'economic war'
entries.summary: Iran has said nations joining US economic sanctions against it would be considered enemies. Earlier this week, President Trump had announced what he called the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Iran has said nations joining US economic sanctions against it would be considered enemies. Earlier this week, President Trump had announced what he called the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran.

Iran on Saturday warned countries against joining the United States' campaign to isolate the Iranian economy.

"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, on state television.

"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.

As the war nears its six-month anniversary, US President Donald Trump announced earlier this week what he called the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran.

Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake," said Rezaei.

US urges others to back Iran sanctions

Washington has also called on other governments to join its efforts to ramp up economic pressure against Iran.

But China, one of Iran's top strategic partners, has criticized the new campaign, arguing that "sanctions and pressure will not help resolve the issue."

"China calls on all relevant parties to take responsible measures and resolve the problem through political and diplomatic means," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian told reporters on Friday.

The United Arab Emirates, a major trading partner for sanctioned Iran, already announced on Wednesday that it was cutting all financial and economic ties with Tehran until further notice.

The decision was made in "light of escalations that undermine peace and security in the region," the UAE said in a statement. 

US tells allies: 'With us or against us'

Talks between Washington and Tehran remain on hold after nearly six months of war since the US and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday to give further details of the economic measures against Iran.

"This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us,” Bessent said.

Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Iran has faced almost 50 years of near-continuous economic sanctions.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Canada to hit back with retaliatory tariffs after US trade talks fail
entries.summary: The trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington has escalated as Canada announced tariffs on US products. The move comes in response to the US saying that tariffs would follow the collapse of talks.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

The trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington has escalated as Canada announced tariffs on US products. The move comes in response to the US saying that tariffs would follow the collapse of talks.

In an ongoing trade dispute with the United States, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.

The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.

"Canada will match Washington's new ⁠tariffs ​dollar for dollar in order to protect ​Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.

"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day," he said.

While the US had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."

He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.

What products are affected by the tariffs?

The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing ‌rods, and hockey ​equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."

"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

How have Canadian and US politicians reacted?

Doug Ford, the premier of Canada's most populous province Ontario and one of the most vocal opponents of Trump's tariffs, slammed the proposed trade deal and backed Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and ​manufacturing sector," Ford said on Saturday.

In the US, Democratic lawmakers and governors have blamed Trump for the escalating trade conflict.

"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.

Friendly ties turned sour

The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from Washington and Ottawa appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.

According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.

The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had.

US President Donald Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the US.

He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Cargo vessel sinks off Indian coast
entries.summary: The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner reportedly had a crew of 24, at least two of whom appear to have been rescued. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.
entries.content:
August 22, 2026

The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner reportedly had a crew of 24, at least two of whom appear to have been rescued. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.

A cargo ship has sunk off the eastern coast of India, the country's coast guard said. The Panama-flagged vessel Ocean Winner had 24 crew on board, at least two of whom were reportedly rescued.

The crew included 20 Chinese nationals, three seamen from Myanmar and one from Bangladesh, Indian officials said.

Why the ship sank remains unclear.

According to officials cited in the Indian Express, the ship was about 240 nautical miles (444 kilometers, 276 miles) off the coast of Odisha. A joint operation by the Indian Coast Guard and the country's navy was underway to find more survivors.

The Hindustan Times reported local Paradip police official Sanjay Negi saying that rescue teams would reach the site "by tomorrow morning" and that other vessels in the vicinity had been alerted to help with the rescue effort.

According to ship-tracking app MarineTraffic, the Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore from Paradip port in Odisha to Singapore.

entries.title: Nigeria: Jihadis kidnap dozens during Friday prayers
entries.summary: Witnesses said men carrying guns and machetes set upon two villages in Niger State. Many details about the attack have yet to be confirmed by police.
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria: Jihadis kidnap dozens during Friday prayers

August 22, 2026

Witnesses said men carrying guns and machetes set upon two villages in Niger State. Many details about the attack have yet to be confirmed by police.

Extremists attacked and abducted a number of worshipers in Nigeria's Niger State, authorities said on Saturday.

Police said the armed men attacked a number of villages in the Borgu Local Government Area before storming mosque in the village Kpenya during Friday prayers.

"People were abducted while praying at a Juma’at mosque on Friday," Borgu area council chair Abdullahi Mohammed Nasir told the Associated Press.

"That was when the bad people came and surrounded the mosque and took them away."

Some witnesses recounted extreme violence.

"Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group [...] in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us," one survivor told the AFP news agency. "They slaughtered some of our people, saying we are not practicing the true teachings of Islam."

Local residents told the AFP and Reuters news agencies that dozens of people — as many as 60 — were kidnapped.

Witnesses also told AFP that the armed men killed several people, although according to police, "the developing report indicated that no life ‌was ​lost."

Who was responsible for the attack?

No group claimed responsibilityfor the attack in the day that followed and police have not identified the culprits.

One witness told AFP that the gunmen belonged to Lakurawa — an increasingly radical outfit that researchers link to the "Islamic State Sahel Province" group.

Another resident told AFP that the attackers were Ansaru, which split from Boko Haram and is now aligned with al-Qaeda.

Witnesses also said that a third, rival jihadi group known as Mahmuda clashed with the attackers and allowed some of the abductees to escape.

Although jihadi attacks have declined in Nigeria since the height of Boko Haram's insurgency last decade, the military and police remain overstretched as they face multiple, sometimes overlapping conflicts.

In addition to jihadist insurgency in the north, parts of Nigeria also face violence and kidnappings from non-ideological gangs known locally as "bandits."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Germany news: Friedrich Merz visits area struck by fires
entries.summary: Chancellor Merz thanked firefighters who tackled recent devastating blazes in western Germany. Meanwhile, a German Cup soccer match ended in a mass brawl with over 100 injuries. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Friedrich Merz visits area struck by fires

Published August 22, 2026last updated August 23, 2026

Chancellor Merz thanked firefighters who tackled recent devastating blazes in western Germany. Meanwhile, a German Cup soccer match ended in a mass brawl with over 100 injuries. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Chancellor

    Friedrich Merz traveled to the Hürtgenwald region, where fires raged for several days

  • Merz thanked firefighters and rescue workers who

    battled the fire for several days before extinguishing it

  • A German Cup match between southwestern rivals Waldhof Mannheim and Kaiserslautern ends in a mass brawl with dozens of injuries and arrests

  • Germany's antisemitism commissioner, Felix Klein, calls for criminal laws to be strengthened to include penalties for pro-Hamas demonstrators

  • Foreign Minister

    Johann Wadephul is in Kyiv as Ukraine prepares to celebrate its independence and Russian missiles rain down on the country

This is a roundup of the main headlines in and about Germany on the weekend of August 22-23, 2026:

Skip next section We're pausing our coverage

We're pausing our coverage

We're pausing our Germany news blog for the time being.

Stay tuned for more coverage in this blog later on Sunday with DW!

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Industry and residents clash over water near Berlin

IN DEPTH: Industry and residents clash over water near Berlin

The state surrounding Berlin is drying out, but local Tesla and Red Bull plants are looking to expand. Is Brandenburg running out of water to share?

Learn more about the drought affecting Berlin and the surrounding areas in this report by DW's Anne-Sophie Brändin.

Skip next section Merz says forest fires 'a consequence of climate change'

Merz says forest fires 'a consequence of climate change'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thanked local firefighters for their efforts battling last week's dramatic forest fire in western Germany's Eifel region and stressed that such fires are a consequence of climate change. 

"We have to expect such events more often," he said during a visit to the communities affected by the fires. "This is climate change."

"I want to tell all those climate change deniers: Look at what's happening here," he added.

Merz said he would do everything possible to combat climate change but stressed that "we also have to live with climate change."

When it comes to climate policy, Merz's CDU has stressed the importance of market-based strategies rather than bans to protect the environment.

He was met with whistles and boos from people holding signs and saying Merz's government has not adequately addressed the climate crisis.

The chancellor thanked the firefighters and all other local groups that helped fight the  Hürtgenwald fire that raged for a week, forcing the evacuation of entire villages before it was finally extinguished late last week. 

It was Merz's first public appearance since July 29, when he left for his summer vacation. He previously thanked emergency workers for their "tireless effort" on X.

Opposition parties criticized his prolonged absence while the country was grappling with heat waves and forest fires and suggested he was not taking climate change seriously.

Skip next section Magdeburg marks Pride parade ahead of crucial election

Magdeburg marks Pride parade ahead of crucial election

Under the slogan "Vote for Love," around 3,000 people took part in a pride parade in the eastern German city of Magdeburg. The city is the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, which will hold state elections on September 6 that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win.

The AfD promotes a traditional heterosexual family model and is at times critical of the LGBTQ+ community.

The parade's organizers said Saturday’s event was a show of support for democracy, diversity and an open society.

While it was Magdeburg’s 30th Pride parade, this year was the first time it was held on a central square in front of the state parliament, in part to increase political visibility ahead of the election but also to help with security measures.

Last month, a deadly attack on the Berlin Pride Parade left one person dead and injured many others.

Several other cities in Germany also held their pride parade on Saturday. In Bremen, around 33,000 people marched under the slogan "Generations Full of Pride — Happy, Visible, Strong."

Skip next section Conservative local candidate sparks controversy with 'MILF' necklace

Conservative local candidate sparks controversy with 'MILF' necklace

Corinna Jodeit, a candidate from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in local elections outside Bremen, has caused a stir with her official campaign portrait.

Jodeit is running for a seat on the Wildeshausen city council and can be seen wearing a gold necklace prominently featuring the English-language acronym MILF on posters for the September 13 vote.

The term is an abbreviation for the phrase "Mother I'd like to f---."

The candidate herself said that although the term is "naturally provocative," the necklace is "just a piece of jewelry" that emphasizes her independence.

"I'm happy to be a mum, but there's more to me than that," she told the Wildeshausener Zeitung newspaper, admitting that she had considered removing the necklace for the photo but added that she felt it would have been inauthentic.

Comments below an Instagram post by the paper garnered strong opinions, offering both support and critique, with some readers calling the situation "embarrassing" and "inappropriate" and others saying they found it "hot" and "funny."

Skip next section German finance minister calls for windfall tax on oil profits

German finance minister calls for windfall tax on oil profits

German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called for a tax on windfall profits currently being racked up by large multinational oil companies.  

"We must address the problem of high energy prices by discussing an EU-wide framework for taxing windfall profits," Klingbeil wrote in an open letter also signed by several European counterparts.

Klingbeil said he has often raised the issue of energy company rip-offs at the Finance Ministry in Berlin and has now joined his colleagues to call on Ireland's Finance Minister Simon Harris to put the topic on the EU agenda "as soon as possible."

Ireland currently holds the EU's rotating presidency. 

The next meeting of European finance ministers is scheduled to take place in Dublin on September 18 and 19.

Although finance ministers acknowledge that the main price driver at the moment is the US-Israeli war on Iran, they point out that "oil companies are reporting strong overall profitability and margins on refined products, which — albeit possibly influenced by product-specific bottlenecks — exceed the rise in crude oil prices."

"Dissatisfaction with the rising cost of living is growing not only in Germany and Europe, but worldwide," as government interventions fail to ease the burden of higher fuel prices on taxpayers, the ministers wrote.

The ministers are now calling on those who profit from the current crisis in the Middle East to "pay their share to ease the burden on the public at large."

Klingbeil and his colleagues say the EU should make available its findings from 2022 research on "targeting the foreign profits of multi-national oil companies" and how they can be taxed.

According to aid organization Oxfam, the world's six largest fossil fuel companies — BP, Chevron, Eni, ExxonMobil, Shell and TotalEnergies — registered €40 billion in profits in the second quarter of 2026. Total profit is forecast to hit €147 billion for the year.

Germany's federal government, like those of Klingbeil's partners, has so far refused to level windfall oil profit taxes.

The European Commission has also poured cold water on the concept, saying it has no plans to introduce any scheme on excessive profits.

Skip next section Massive pay gap between German, foreign workers in Germany

Massive pay gap between German, foreign workers in Germany

Germany's Labor Ministry released data on Saturday showing a 23.6% pay gap between German and foreign full-time workers in 2025.

The data was released in response to a parliamentary inquiry posed by far-right opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD).

Accordingly, although wage growth grew across the board, median full-time monthly pay for Germans was €4,396 ($5,138), whereas foreign full-time employees pulled in €3,358.

The numbers track with trends seen since 2020.

Overall, Labor Ministry stats show that 30.6% of foreign workers earned low wages as compared to 12.3% of Germans.

The AfD launched its query to poke holes in Berlin's immigration policies, which it claims are smothering wage growth, though that is not made clear by the data.

A separate study by the Institute for Employment Research said the gap could be because "immigrants are less likely to be employed in high-paying sectors or positions."

The Federal Employment Agency said earnings depend heavily on a person's education, qualifications and professional job experience.

In 2025, workers without vocational qualifications earned a median wage of €3,133, while full-time employees with recognized vocational qualifications earned €4,069 and college graduates earned €6,146.

Skip next section Germany's FAZ newspaper slams Russian arrest warrant for correspondent

Germany's FAZ newspaper slams Russian arrest warrant for correspondent

Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on Saturday slammed a Russian Interior Ministry arrest warrant for the paper's Balkans correspondent Michael Martens, as "an attempt to intimidate a German journalist and the free press."

The paper accused Moscow of seeking to curtail free speech through threat of criminal punishment. 

"Freedom of the press is non-negotiable," said the FAZ, "It applies even when questions or reports provoke criticism."

The paper said it flatly rejects any attempt to obstruct independent journalism.

Russia issued the warrant over Martens' phrasing in posing a question to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an August 8, 2026, press conference in the Serbian capital, Belgrade.

Mertens asked Zelenskyy what Europeans could do "to help you kill more Russians," which FAZ management says could have been formulated differently, acknowledging that the phrasing left the issue open to "misinterpretation."

The paper said, "We have clarified this and expressed our regret at the wording."

Last week, Russia issued its warrant for Martens' arrest for "public incitement to hatred and hostility." If found guilty, he would face six years in prison.

The Russian Embassy in Berlin has asked public prosecutors in the German capital to look into the situation, saying Martens' remarks "regarding the possibility of 'aiding and abetting the murder of Russians' as well as the lack of a public apology," suggest the wording "was chosen deliberately and intentionally."

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described Martens' words as "unacceptable" and "criminal."

Skip next section Germany mulls constitutional protections for LGBTQ+ people after Berlin Pride attack

Germany mulls constitutional protections for LGBTQ+ people after Berlin Pride attack

Germany's Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig is calling for an amendment to the country's constitution, known as the German Basic Law, to specifically protect LGBTQ+ people.

"I am in favour of amending Article 3(3) of the Basic Law to include a ban on discrimination on the grounds of sexual identity," Hubig told the Rheinische Post newspaper in an interview published on Saturday.

Hubig, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said there were reservations within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives, but there were also encouraging signs.

German Basic Law prohibits the disadvantage or preferential treatment of people on grounds such as their ancestry, language, homeland or origin, their faith, religion or political views. "It is only logical to also prohibit unequal treatment on the grounds of sexual identity," said Hubig.

Hubig's comments come after a man drove his car into a crowd on the sidelines of Pride festivities in Berlin, one of the largest LGBTQ events in Europe.

The suspected attacker, Abdul Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese background, was shot dead by police the day after the attack following a major manhunt.

Skip next section Germany's antisemitism commissioner calls for tougher laws for Hamas supporters

Germany's antisemitism commissioner calls for tougher laws for Hamas supporters

Germany's Federal Antisemitism Commissioner Felix Klein on Saturday called for harsher laws and punishment for those supporting militant Palestinian groups such as Hamas.

In an interview published in the Saturday edition of the daily Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper, Klein said he hopes Chancellor Merz and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig will strengthen existing laws and called for anyone demonstrating in support of the Palestinian militant group Hamas — considered a terrorist group by Israel, the US, Germany and many other nations — to face at least six months in jail.

"If the person is a foreign national without secure residence status," added Klein, "they should be deported after being convicted and serving their sentence."

He also demanded customs authorities be given expanded powers to disrupt the financing of terrorist organizations.

While praising the work done combating antisemitism through education, Klein also called for rigorous, mandatory teacher training. "Anyone susceptible to antisemitism has no place in the teaching profession," he said, calling for disciplinary consequences for teachers expressing antisemitic sentiments.

Klein said Jewish life in Germany must be presented in a positive light and that Judaism is about more than antisemitism, the Holocaust and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Felix Klein is leaving his current post, which he has held since 2018, to serve as Germany's ambassador to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in Paris.

Skip next section Over 100 injured in mass soccer brawl at German Cup match

Over 100 injured in mass soccer brawl at German Cup match

Some 35 police officers and 85 fans were injured in a massive brawl during a soccer match on Friday evening in the southwestern city of Mannheim say local officials, with several people hospitalized. 

More than 1,400 police and security officers were on hand for the German Cup game between local rivals Waldhof Mannheim and 1. FC Kaiserslautern. Officials say 23,500 fans were at the sold-out game, 3,500 of them supporters of visiting Kaiserslautern.

Those fans began shooting fireworks at Mannheim players at the end of normal time with the match goalless. Mannheim fans rushed onto the pitch in response, which in turn brought out mounted police and security officers.

"The intense preparations by all participating institutions and the close cooperation among all those involved paid off. Our tactical plan worked perfectly," said Mannheim Police Chief Michael Reichert after the melee.

Manuel Hagel, Baden-Württemberg's interior minister, said, "Anyone who abuses soccer as a stage for violent outbursts, deliberately puts other fans in danger, and — above all — injures security personnel is not a fan, but a criminal. That is exactly how we will treat these individuals in order to enforce law and order in our stadiums."

Police say they have launched investigations into "insults, various assault charges, property damage, breach of the peace, physical assault on police officers, and violations of the Explosives Act."

Several football fans were detained, German news agency DPA reported.

The German Football Association (DFB) has promised a full report into the incident.

Ibrahim Kanate scored in the last minute of extra time to give Kaiserslautern a 1-0 win. The second-division side advances to the second round of the Cup.

Skip next section Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visits Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks

Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visits Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul arrived in Kyiv by a special train on Saturday morning, ahead of Ukraine's 35th independence day.

His visit comes as two Ukrainians were killed overnight in Russian attacks, and a day after at least 15 were killed and more than 100 injured in an attack on a shopping center in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's home town.

Skip next section Merz to thank firefighters for 'tireless' effort

Merz to thank firefighters for 'tireless' effort

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to interrupt his summer vacation to travel to the state of North Rhine-Westphalia on Saturday, where he will thank rescue workers and firefighters for their efforts battling last week's devastating forest fire in the western Eifel region's Hürtgenwald — the largest fire in the state's history.

The Hürtgenwald fire raged for a week, forcing the evacuation of entire villages before it could be extinguished two days ago.

Merz will speak with volunteers at the scene to get a picture of the firefighting and reconstruction efforts on the ground.

The appearance is Merz's first in public since July 29, when he left for his summer vacation. He previously thanked workers for their "tireless effort" on X.

His lack of visibility as Germany struggled with historic fires and an ongoing heatwave earned him criticism from the opposition, who accused him of not taking climate change seriously.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

Today we will cover Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to North Rhine-Westphalia, where he is expected to thank firefighters and rescue workers who "worked tirelessly" combating recent wildfires in the Hürtgenwald region of the Eifel. 

We will also be following Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul's trip to Ukraine, where Kyiv is set to celebrate its independence from the Soviet Union as its successor state, Russia, prosecutes its over four-year invasion with devastating nightly missile and drone attacks.

Germany's antisemitism commissioner has called for the compulsory training of teachers and the inclusion of the history of Jewish life in school curricula while at the same time demanding jail for those who espouse antisemitic ideas or openly support Palestinian militant groups such as Hamas.

And a German Cup match between rivals Mannheim and Kaiserslautern was briefly suspended as fans stormed the pitch in a mass brawl that ended with injuries and arrests.

Follow DW here for these stories and the rest of the news in Germany on Saturday.

entries.title: Kazakhstan's future after the elections: Russia, EU or China
entries.summary: Kazakhstan, where power is being continuously consolidated in the president's hands, will have to continue its tough balancing act between the EU, Russia and China following the parliamentary elections this Sunday.
entries.content:
Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan's future after the elections: Russia, EU or China

August 22, 2026

Kazakhstan, where power is being continuously consolidated in the president's hands, will have to continue its tough balancing act between the EU, Russia and China following the parliamentary elections this Sunday.

On August 23, Kazakhstan, a former Soviet country that has recently adopted a new constitution, will hold elections to its parliament.

The legislative body will be transformed from a two-chamber to a single-chamber system. Citizens will elect 145 members of parliament via party lists. All seven registered parties have been admitted to the election, including the ruling party, Adilet (which translates to "Justice").

But the election result is the least of the campaign's intrigues. Experts DW interviewed agree that no party other than President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's Adilet stands a chance of winning.

Consolidation of power in the president's hands

Luca Anceschi, Professor of Eurasian Studies at the University of Glasgow, Scotland, suggests that the new parliament will do the same as the previous one, "which is pretty much to represent whatever the regime wants them to do."

In his view, one should not expect representatives of the genuine opposition to be elected to parliament.

Stefan Meister, Head of the Center for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), shares this assessment. He says the ruling party is likely to win the election, a scenario also reflected in recent opinion polls.

Both experts agree that these elections are intended to consolidate Tokayev's power and further weaken the bloc led by  Nursultan Nazarbayev, the country's president from 1991-2019. 

Constitutional amendments approved earlier allow Tokayev to seek another seven-year presidential term in 2029 and replace the two-chamber parliament with a single-chamber assembly called the Kurultai.

According to former Kazakhstani senator Zauresh Battalova, who now heads the NGO Foundation for the Development of Parliamentarism in Kazakhstan, what matters is not the number of chambers in parliament, but "the scope of its powers, its autonomy and its ability to oversee the executive branch of government."

The new constitution has changed not only the structure of parliament but also the way its members are elected. Independent candidates are no longer allowed to run under the current electoral system. Zauresh Battalova sees this as one of the factors limiting voters' political choice.

"The election will be held exclusively on the basis of party lists, in the absence of a political opposition and with limited party competition. The scope for genuine political choice remains extremely narrow," she told DW.

Kazakhstan's democratic backlash: Will Europe react?

Meister and Anceschi both say that one should not expect any reaction from European Union members or the European Commission to the deterioration in political freedoms in Kazakhstan.

Meister points out that, since the start of the war in Ukraine, the EU has adopted a more pragmatic approach towards Central Asian states. Europe is now interested in developing trade routes as an alternative to those via Russia, as well as in the region's abundant resources. In his view, the only bodies likely to react to the current situation in Kazakhstan are civil society organizations, the European Parliament or the Council of Europe.

"The days when the European Union and individual EU member states were more critical of the rule of law and governance in Central Asia are gone, unfortunately," Anceschi says.

The University of Glasgow professor notes that an authoritarian backslide is taking place not only in Kazakhstan but also in other EU partner countries.

As for Kazakhstan itself, says Meister, it remains the least repressive authoritarian country in the region, with at least some space for civil society, albeit one that is narrowing.

"Wherever you buy your oil and gas from, you are never going to buy it from a democracy ― unless it is Norway. So, in that sense, there is not much of a choice," Anceschi says.

In 2025, Kazakhstan became the second-largest oil exporter to the EU, with a total share of 12.8%, amounting to 55.8 million tons of crude oil, surpassed only by the United States, according to the European Council of the EU.

The future of Kazakhstan's foreign policy

Experts acknowledge that Kazakhstan has managed to remain neutral in the standoff between Russia and Europe against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine. Maintaining this course may prove difficult.

"They are affected by the conflict, but they are not participating," says Anceschi, describing the country's current position as a "geopolitical comfort zone."

Kazakhstan has not officially opposed the European sanctions against Russia, nor has it joined them.

"Of course, it is a task with only one ultimate goal, which is the preservation of authoritarian rule," Anceschi says. "So even in this case, foreign policy is becoming an instrument for achieving internal stability."

Meister, in turn, draws attention to the increasing level of cooperation between the Central Asian states, which, facing significant external pressure, tend to act as a single bloc while actively seeking to reduce tensions among themselves. He suggests that Kazakhstan is interested in diversifying its external relations not only with the EU, Russia and China, but also with other world powers, such as Arab or East Asian states.

According to Meister, Kazakhstan "does not want to be too dependent on Russia ― it has seen what Russia is doing in Ukraine ― and it does not want to be dependent on China."

So, the country is looking for alternatives, and Europe could be one of them, both as a market for its resources and as a potential investor in Kazakhstan's economy.

This article was adapted from Russian.

entries.title: Spain battles forest fire a short drive from flash flood
entries.summary: The blaze, near Valencia, forced more than 1,000 people from their homes. In nearby Catalonia, civil defense teams carried out 200 rescue operations after floods trapped residents in cars and homes.
entries.content:
August 22, 2026

The blaze, near Valencia, forced more than 1,000 people from their homes. In nearby Catalonia, civil defense teams carried out 200 rescue operations after floods trapped residents in cars and homes.

A forest fire in eastern Spain sparked the evacuation of around 1,000 people on Saturday, authorities said.

The blaze is one of hundreds that firefighters across Europe have been battling this summer amid record high temperatures along the Mediterranean and elsewhere.

Barely 150 kilometers (93 miles) away on the Costa Dorada, flash floods trapped people in cars, toppled walls and forced the evacuation of a campsite.

What do we know about the fire?

The fire is burning close to Gatova, an inland village with a population of 450, northwest of Valencia.

TV footage showed the flames were moving close to built-up areas.

Spain's Military Emergency Unit UME posted a video to X showing its firefighters working in the darkness to douse the flames.

Several firefighting helicopters and aircraft were also deployed.

Local media reported that the blaze is thought to have been started by a lightning strike late Thursday.

By Friday evening, more than 400 hectares of land had been burnt.

Juan Carlos Valderrama, Valencia autonomous community's civil protection minister, said buses were on standby to help residents without their own vehicles to leave their homes.

What's the latest on the floods?

Further north, along Spain's Costa Dorada, heavy rain overnight flooded streets and caused the collapse of two walls, injuring at least seven people, officials said.

According to local media, roads in the coastal towns El Vendrell, Coma-ruga and Torredembarra in the Cataloniaregion were partially submerged.

The Meteorological Service of Catalonia said several towns recorded nearly 200 liters per square meter in just a few hours.

On Saturday morning, the agency warned of more heavy rainfall for the coastal region.

Local media reported that several people got trapped in their vehicles during the flooding.

A regional emergency official said firefighters had carried out more than 200 missions to rescue people from vehicles and flooded buildings.

Three people were injured when a wall collapsed at the port of Roda de Bera, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) southwest of Barcelona, emergency services said.

Another wall collapse at a nearby campsite injured two others.

Around 300 people staying at the campsite were evacuated, with many sheltering at a nearby sports center, officials said.

entries.title: Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record
entries.summary: The Chinese humanoid robot "Lightning" ran a 100-meter trial race faster than human world-record holder Usain Bolt. A year ago, humanoid robots struggled to finish a race.
entries.content:
August 22, 2026

The Chinese humanoid robot "Lightning" ran a 100-meter trial race faster than human world-record holder Usain Bolt. A year ago, humanoid robots struggled to finish a race.

A Chinese humanoid robot finished a 100-meter practice race in just 9.32 seconds, beating the human world record, Chinese media reported on Saturday.

That put the robot, called Lightning, at the finish line 0.26 seconds faster than Jamaican Usain Bolt, who set a world record at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin in 2009 with a 100m time of 9.58 seconds.

Lightning's preparatory run was for the second World Humanoid Robot Games that opened in Beijing on Saturday.

The sporting event is one of a kind where technology companies — mostly Chinese — and university groups gather to show off the many tasks their robots can do.

Lightning's extraordinary race to the finish line is a big marker of progress in the field of artificial intelligence because the best of humanoid robots were struggling to complete a race just last year.

China progressing fast at humanoid robotics

Lightning, developed by Chinese smartphone maker Honor, also won the Beijing half-marathon (21 kilometers) earlier this April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds.

That was several minutes faster than the human world record holder, Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo, who ran the same distance in 57 minutes, 20 seconds, in Lisbon this March.

Lightning stood 169 centimeters tall and had 95-centimeter ​legs at ⁠the half marathon.

Jacob Kiplimo of Uganda holds the men's half-marathon record with a time of 57 minutes and 20 seconds. Ethiopia's Letesenbet Gidey holds the women's record, having finished in 1 hour, 2 minutes, 52 seconds.

In a feat its human competitors would have a difficult time replicating, Lightning's legs were lengthened by ⁠10 cm ​to 1.05 meters ahead of the World Humanoid Robot Games, China Central Television reported.

entries.title: Myanmar military airstrike kills 14 at Buddhist monastery: reports
entries.summary: Around 100 people were attending a meditation retreat in central Myanmar when the building was targeted by military planes, witnesses said.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar airstrike kills 14 at Buddhist monastery: reports

August 22, 2026

Around 100 people were attending a meditation retreat in central Myanmar when the building was targeted by military planes, witnesses said.

At least 14 people were killed when a military airstrike hit a Buddhist monastery in Myanmar's central Sagaing region, an opposition group and local witnesses said Saturday.

Friday's attack, by the ruling military regime that seized power in a 2021 coup, is the latest deadly assault on pro-democracy forces in the Southeast Asian country's ongoing civil war.

What do we know about the airstrike on the monastery in Myanmar?

The strike happened in Swel Le Oh village, Myaung township, in central Myanmar, said Nway Oo, a spokesman for an anti-government resistance group.

The village is about 75 kilometers (45 miles) west of Mandalay, the country's second largest city.

Nway Oo, from the Civil Defense and Security Organization of Myaung Township, or CDSOM, said the dead included three women and that 20 others were wounded.

The Associated Press spoke to a villager who confirmed the death toll and said that a military jet dropped two bombs 15 minutes apart.

The villager said the second strike damaged a nearby house.

Victims were civilians attending a retreat

More than 100 people were taking part in a weeklong meditation retreat to mark Buddhist Lent, the villager added.

AFP news agency cited Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel, as saying: "It wasn't a mistaken target; they intentionally attacked a monastery."

The military government has yet to confirm the strike.

Myanmar's military has often used airstrikes to counter opposition forces, especially in Sagaing region, a stronghold of armed resistance.

UN flags sharp rise in airstrikes

A United Nations investigation team said last week it had observed a notable increase in aerial attacks over much of the past year.

The UN's Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) accused the military-backed government of "indiscriminate and intentional aerial attacks against civilians."

Last month, conflict monitoring group ACLED accused the regime of adopting "a terror strategy" that it said focuses on "civilian infrastructure and social gatherings, such as weddings and religious festivals, to maximize psychological impact."

Myanmar government defends strikes

On Sunday, Myanmar’s foreign ministry rejected the IIMM report, insisting that its operations were in response to insurgents and terrorist groups.

The ministry said it uses maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.

Myanmar's army took power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.

Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was detained and sentenced to lengthy prison terms on multiple charges widely viewed as politically motivated. She was moved to house arrest in May.

After a brutal crackdown on peaceful demonstrations, many opponents of military rule armed themselves and plunged large parts of the country into conflict.

More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed on all sides over the past five years, according to ACLED.

Myanmar held elections this year, which were widely condemned as a sham.

The polls culminated in the chief of the former junta, General Min Aung Hlaing, being appointed president, as the military regime sought to present itself as a civilian government.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Small German airplane crashes in Croatia, killing 2
entries.summary: The two-seater motor glider went down in the Velebit mountains, near Zadar, killing both passengers.
entries.content:
Germany

Small German airplane crashes in Croatia, killing 2

August 22, 2026

The two-seater motor glider went down in the Velebit mountains, near Zadar, killing both passengers.

Two people were killed when a small aircraft registered in Germany crashed near Croatia's coastal city of Zadar, local media reported on Saturday.

Croatian police said the two-seater motor glider, which can fly with a small engine or glide without one, went down in the Velebit mountains on Friday.

The long, rugged mountain range runs parallel to the Adriatic coast.

Authorities said the Diamond HK36 Super Dimona was en route from the Czech Republic to Zadar when it crashed.

According to media reports, contact with the aircraft was lost just after 4 p.m. local time (1400 GMT/UTC).

What do we know about the plane crash in Croatia?

Police said the wreckage, along with the bodies of two passengers, was found after a lengthy search.

Challenging terrain, along with heavy rain, wind and fog, meant it took nearly six hours to reach the location.

Croatian media outlet Jutarnji list cited the mountain rescue agency as describing the conditions as "extremely difficult."

The fog, which reduced visibility to around 2 meters, also prevented the deployment of search drones, Jutarnji list reported.

The agency sent a 35-person rescue team to the crash site, local media said.

Officials have not announced the victims' identities or nationalities

German news agency DPA cited the Czech Foreign Ministry as saying the victims were not Czech citizens.
